title: How much household bleach to add to make water safe to drink

answer: If the water is cloudy, first let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter. Disinfection does not work as well when water is cloudy or colored.
1 quart or 1 liter of water: add 2 drops of bleach (6% or 8.25% strength).
1 gallon of water: add 8 drops of 6% bleach.
1 gallon of water with 8.25% bleach: EPA says 6 drops; CDC says 8 drops (CDC gives 8 drops for any 5%-9% bleach).
Cloudy, colored or very cold water: EPA says double the amount of bleach. CDC says 16 drops per gallon for cloudy tap water.
Stir, then let the water stand for at least 30 minutes before using it.
The water should have a slight chlorine smell. If it does not, repeat the dose and let it stand for another 15 minutes before use.
If the chlorine taste is too strong, pour the water from one clean container to another and let it stand for a few hours before use.
No dropper: wet a cloth or stick with bleach and let it drip into the water.
warnings: Only use regular, unscented chlorine bleach. Do not use scented, color safe, or bleaches with added cleaners.
Use fresh bleach, or bleach stored at room temperature for less than 1 year.
Boiling is the best method: CDC says boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites, while bleach kills most viruses and bacteria. Use bleach if you cannot boil the water.
Chlorine is relatively ineffective against Cryptosporidium. Where it is suspected in the water, boiling is the recommended method.
Bleach will not destroy other contaminants such as heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals.
Do not use water with floating material in it, or water that has a dark color or a questionable odor.

quotes.text: If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter.
Disinfection does not work as well when water is cloudy or colored. If water is cloudy, let it settle. Then filter the water through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter.

Use the table below as a guide to decide the amount of bleach you should add to the water, for example, 8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, to each gallon of water. Double the amount of bleach if the water is cloudy, colored, or very cold.
Volume of Water | Amount of 6% Bleach to Add* | Amount of 8.25% Bleach to Add* | 1 quart/liter | 2 drops | 2 drops | 1 gallon | 8 drops | 6 drops

This method will kill most viruses and bacteria. Add 8 drops or a little less than 1/8 of a teaspoon of 5%-9% unscented household bleach to 1 gallon water. For cloudy tap water, use 16 drops or ¼ teaspoon.
Stir and let stand for 30 minutes. The water should have a slight chlorine odor. If it doesn’t, repeat the dosage and let stand for another 15 minutes before use.
Mix well. Wait at least 30 minutes before using.
If the chlorine taste is too strong, pour the water from one clean container to another and let it stand for a few hours before use.
If a dropper is not available, wet a cloth or stick with bleach and allow it to drip into the water.

Disinfect water using household bleach, if you can’t boil water. Only use regular, unscented chlorine bleach products that are suitable for disinfection and sanitization as indicated on the label. The label may say that the active ingredient contains 6 or 8.25% of sodium hypochlorite. Do not use scented, color safe, or bleaches with added cleaners.
Locate a fresh liquid chlorine bleach or liquid chlorine bleach that is stored at room temperatures for less than one year.
This method will kill bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Boiling water is the best method.

Where Cryptosporidium parvum is suspected to be present in untreated water, boiling is the recommended emergency water treatment method because of the relative ineffectiveness of chlorine and iodine against that organism.
However, boiling or disinfection will not destroy other contaminants, such as heavy metals, salts, and most other chemicals.

You can also use river or lake water. It is generally better to use flowing water than still, stagnant water. However, do not use water with floating material in it or water that has a dark color or questionable odor. Regardless of the source, treat the water by following the instructions on the main page above.

conflict: 8.25% bleach per gallon: the EPA (2026) table says 6 drops; the CDC (2024) sheet says 8 drops for any 5%-9% bleach. Cloudy water: EPA says double the dose (also for colored or very cold water), which is 12 drops per gallon of 8.25% bleach; CDC says 16 drops per gallon for cloudy tap water. The two agree for 6% bleach (8 drops per gallon, 16 if cloudy) and on the 30-minute wait. The card shows both where they differ; the owner must choose. Other kit documents: TB MED 577 (2010) and ATP 3-50.21 (2018) give 2 drops per quart for 5% / 5.25% bleach with a 30-minute wait (consistent), but ATP 3-50.21 says 'If cold and cloudy, wait 60 minutes' instead of doubling the dose. Parasites: CDC says bleach 'will kill most viruses and bacteria' and names parasites only for boiling; the card states the two CDC sentences side by side and does not itself say bleach fails against parasites (only the TB MED 577 Cryptosporidium sentence says so). HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) and FEMA P-2064 (2020) were searched: neither gives a bleach dose for drinking water.
